name: Paracas culture
info: The Paracas culture was an Andean society on the south coast of Peru, in today’s Ica Region, from about 800 to 100 BCE, known for the embroidered textiles of its mummy bundles, its irrigation and its skull surgery.

facts.homeland: The south coast of Peru, in today’s Ica Region: the Paracas Peninsula, with the Paracas Cavernas tombs and the Wari Kayan necropolis on Cerro Colorado; the Chincha Valley, probably its political centre, with Cerro del Gentil; the Ica, Pisco and Palpa valleys and Ocucaje.
facts.period: About 800 to 100 BCE; pottery phases early (840–500 BCE), middle (500–380 BCE) and late (380–260 BCE); burials at Wari Kayan continued until about 250 CE, and the culture is thought to have evolved into the Nazca culture.
facts.known: the Paracas Necropolis textiles and embroideries; mummy bundles; polychrome pottery with post-fire resin painting; trophy heads; artificial cranial deformation; the earliest trepanations in the Americas; irrigation; geoglyphs in Palpa province
facts.sources: Excavations at the Paracas site from the 1920s by Julio Tello; later work in the Chincha Valley, including strontium isotope tests and radiocarbon dates at Cerro del Gentil; studies of the textiles by Anne Paul; skulls from the Paracas Cavernas; drone surveys of geoglyphs in 2018.

t: The Paracas culture flourished on the south coast of Peru from about 800 to 100 BCE as a set of local chiefdoms joined by shared religion and trade, with irrigation systems to raise their harvests.

Its dead were bound in a seated position and wrapped in many layers of finely woven and embroidered cloth, and the Paracas Necropolis textiles are considered among the finest ever produced in the Pre-Columbian Andes.
The Paracas culture is believed to have evolved into the Nazca culture, which shared its religion and carried on its textile making, head-hunting and warfare.
dyk: The Paracas culture shows the earliest trepanations known in the Americas: parts of the skull were scraped and drilled away, and by the healing of the bone nearly 40 per cent of patients survived long-term.
ev: The Paracas culture emerges on the south coast of Peru, within the Chavín sphere of interaction
Cerro del Gentil in the Upper Chincha Valley begins to host feasts for people from across the Paracas sphere
In the middle Paracas period Chavín influence dwindles, and Paracas communities form their own identities and expand their trade
About 420 people are buried in two clusters of pit tombs at the Paracas Necropolis, wrapped in textile mummy bundles
A termination ritual with a great feast and offerings closes Cerro del Gentil
Julio Tello makes the first formal investigations of the Paracas site
Looters plunder the Paracas Necropolis, and its textiles begin to appear on the international market
Drone surveys reveal many geoglyphs in Palpa province, now assigned to the Paracas culture

sections.origins:
The Paracas culture was an Andean society that existed between about 800 BCE and 100 BCE on the south coast of Peru, in what is now the Ica Region. It is named after the Paracas Peninsula, whose large seaside site was first formally investigated in the 1920s by the Peruvian archaeologist Julio Tello, and from whose excavations most of what is known of the Paracas people comes. What they called themselves is unknown.

Early Paracas communities lay within the Chavín sphere of interaction and formed their own versions of the Chavín cult. The first phase of Paracas pottery, dated 840–500 BCE and found along the coast and in the valleys, carries Chavín features: a feline-eagle motif resembles the falcon frieze of the Black and White Portal at Chavín de Huántar, the ceremonial centre of the Chavín culture in the highlands. Paracas emerged as a culture separate from Chavín while borrowing from its art.

In the middle period, 500–380 BCE, Chavín influence dwindled and Paracas communities began to form their own identities, building the religious framework that supported burials with many ceramics. The late phase, 380–260 BCE, saw pottery become more uniform and more people visiting the huacas of the south coast. Scholars order this sequence through the great burial complexes of Paracas Cavernas, the Paracas Necropolis and Ocucaje, built about 2,000 years ago.
sections.society:
Paracas had no central figurehead or government. It was made up of local chiefdoms, joined by shared religion and trade but each keeping its economic and political autonomy, and relations between them were not always peaceful: battle wounds, trophy heads and obsidian knives are found at Paracas sites. Within the wider Paracas sphere, subregions grew up in the Chincha, Ica and Palpa valleys.

The Chincha Valley was probably the political centre, with the Paracas Peninsula perhaps serving mainly as burial grounds and Ica as a peripheral zone. Chincha has many roads, geoglyphs and religious centres where people from the coast and the highlands met, and large ceremonial mounds with little sign of permanent occupation, with farming and fishing in the land around them. Extensive irrigation systems raised harvests here and throughout Paracas settlements.

Cerro del Gentil in the Upper Chincha Valley, dated to about 550–200 BCE, was a platform mound with two sunken courts amid fields, used to host feasts. Strontium isotope tests of its offerings show that people came from long distances, suggesting that distant alliances were built first and on purpose. Most skulls from the Paracas Cavernas were deliberately shaped, mostly in the Tabular Erect form, while the Bilobate form was far more common among women; the shape seems tied neither to social status nor to kinship.
sections.beliefs:
Ceremonial burial was of great importance. The Paracas Cavernas are shaft tombs set into the top of Cerro Colorado, each holding several burials and reused over the centuries; in some cases the heads of the dead were taken out, apparently for rituals, and later reburied. In the necropolis of Wari Kayan, hundreds of burials lay close together in and around abandoned buildings on the hill’s north slope. Each body was bound with cord in a seated position, most facing north across the bay of Paracas, and wrapped in many layers of fine textiles into a conical bundle, beside offerings of pottery, food, baskets and weapons. The dry coast preserved them.

Anne Paul suggests that the bundles’ shape, compared to a seed or a human head, was a conscious choice, the seed a symbol of rebirth, and that the quality of their cloth shows its ceremonial use. Textiles show figures falling or perhaps flying, some with face paint, holding severed trophy heads. Heads were taken in battles or raids, and the head may have been seen as a person’s life force, the place where the spirit dwelt. In the late phase a creature called the “Oculate Being” grew more prominent.

Some archaeologists suggest that an Andean view of gender in four parts, masculine and feminine combined, may explain why men’s and women’s skulls were shaped differently.
sections.arts:
The Paracas Necropolis textiles and embroideries are considered some of the finest ever produced by Pre-Columbian Andean societies, and they are the main works of art by which the culture is known. Weavers used native cotton and the hair of the vicuña, llama and alpaca, wove on backstrap looms, usually in a single colour, and then embroidered the cloth. The earlier linear style followed the weave in running stitches, outlining nested animal figures in red, green, gold and blue; the later block-colour style filled curving part-human, part-animal figures with stem stitches in many vivid colours.

The dyes came from many parts of the Andes. Red came from the cochineal insect, ground with mortar and pestle; yellow from the qolle tree and quico flowers; orange from beard lichen; green from cg’illca mixed with the mineral collpa; and blue from tara. Making a dye could take several hours, and women spent two more boiling and dyeing the fibres before spinning and weaving.

Paracas potters applied a clay slip before firing and often painted afterwards with resin and pigment, making polychrome wares, with geometric, animal and human designs and a recurring full-face feline, that set them apart from Topará and Nazca pottery. Early and middle wares at Ocucaje used iron-rich reds and greens; late ones turned to a more neutral palette. Many of the geoglyphs of Palpa province stand on hillsides, where people could easily have seen them, and their figures may have marked territory.
sections.exchange:
Paracas communities were linked by trade as well as religion. Their textiles combined cotton with camelid fibre, and their dyes came from many altitudes, an example of the reciprocity by which people at lower and higher elevations traded goods. In the middle period they expanded their trade networks. At Cerro del Gentil, isotopes show feasters coming from far away, and offerings included bird feathers from far northern Peru. In the Chincha Valley, roads and ritual centres drew people from both the coast and the highlands.

The earliest Paracas communities lay within the Chavín sphere of interaction, and Chavín motifs shaped their early art. Conflict was part of life too: depressed skull fractures, probably caused by the slings, clubs and atlatls found in mummy bundles, are common in Paracas remains.

The end of Paracas has often been linked to an “invasion” around 150 BCE by the Topará tradition from the north, whose pottery appears at late Paracas and early Nazca sites. That view has recently been questioned. The termination ritual at Cerro del Gentil and at other Chincha Valley sites came before any Topará occupation and shows no sign of resistance to invaders, and the earliest accepted Topará site, Jahuay, was first occupied about 165 years after Cerro del Gentil closed. The decline of Paracas and the passage to Nazca were already under way when the Topará tradition emerged.
sections.legacy:
Scholars such as Helaine Silverman believe that Nazca culture and its iconography evolved from Paracas. Nazca shared its religion and in its early phases carried on Paracas textile making, head-hunting and warfare, and many Wari Kayan bundles hold textiles like those of the early Nazca; burials there continued until about 250 CE. Hendrik Van Gijseghem notes that Paracas remains are scarce in the Río Grande de Nazca drainage, the Nazca heartland, but abundant in the Ica, Pisco and Chincha valleys, and holds that Paracas settlement of the region and later population growth mark the beginning of Nazca society.

The Paracas culture also shows the earliest trepanations in the Americas, made by scraping and drilling away parts of the skull, perhaps to treat fractures. Judging by the bone’s healing, 39 per cent of patients died during or soon after the operation and nearly 40 per cent survived long-term.

The riches of the tombs drew looters. The Paracas Necropolis was heavily looted between 1931 and 1933, during the Great Depression, above all at Wari Kayan; how much was taken is unknown, but Paracas textiles began to appear on the international market, and most of those outside the Andes are believed to have been smuggled out of Peru. In 2018 drone surveys found many geoglyphs in Palpa province, assigned to Paracas and shown to predate the Nazca Lines by a thousand years.

summary: The Paracas culture was a society of local chiefdoms on the south coast of Peru from about 800 to 100 BCE, joined by shared religion, trade and irrigation farming. It is known above all for the mummy bundles of its dead, wrapped in some of the finest textiles of the ancient Andes, and for its shaped skulls and early trepanation. It is believed to have evolved into the Nazca culture.
references: Paul, Anne, Paracas Art and Architecture: Object and Context in South Coastal Peru (University of Iowa Press, 1991)
Anton, Ferdinand, Ancient Peruvian Textiles (Thames & Hudson, 1987)
Lavalle, Jose Antoni, Textile art of Peru (Textil Piura, 1989)
notes: Dates kept: -800 to -100, as in the article’s lede. Conflicts: the first pottery phase begins at 840 BCE, before the 800 BCE start; the last phase ends at 260 BCE; the Necropolis burials are dated ’around 300–200 BCE’ in one place and the burial complexes ’about 2,000 years ago’ in another, while Wari Kayan burials ’continued until approximately 250 CE’, long after the 100 BCE end.

The article twice speaks of an ’Inca valley’ / ’Incan Valley’ in the ceramics section (probably the Ica Valley); I left both phrases out, including the claim that the Oculate Being was ’a major part of the Inca valley’.

The article writes ’Chinca Valley’ once and ’Chincha’ elsewhere; I used Chincha. Lavalle is copied as the article gives him (’Jose Antoni Lavalle’, ’Textile art of Peru’, Textil Piura, 1989, an ASIN instead of an ISBN); the editor may want to check the name.
The geoglyphs are said to ’predate the associated Nazca lines by a thousand years’; this sits oddly with a culture that ended in 100 BCE and passed into Nazca, but I kept it as the article states it.

Trepanation: the article’s frequency estimate of ’around 40%’, which it then calls ’very unlikely’, is left out. That trepanation treated fractures is the article’s ’likely motivation’, hedged as ’perhaps’.

The article does not say who discovered the Necropolis or when, only that Tello first formally investigated the site in the 1920s. Its references section is empty; the three works are from Further reading.

Anne Paul’s seed interpretation: the Textiles section begins ’According to Anne Paul, this shape could have been a conscious choice’, referring back to the bundle shape in the previous section; I joined the two.
